## Conservation of energy

We've got one more application of Reynolds' Transport Theorem: the conservation of energy. Stated in words: the change in energy over time for a mass of material (a "closed" system) equals the sum of the net heat transfer rate in and work rate on the system. Putting this into an equation

$$
\frac{DE_\text{sys}}{Dt} = \underbrace{\dot{Q} + \dot{W}}_{\color{green}{\text{net "in"}}} \overset{\color{red}{\text{RTT}}}{=} \int_{CV} \frac{\partial}{\partial t}(\rho e)\, dV + \int_{CS} \rho e\,(\mathbf{u}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{n}})\, dS
$$

where the right-hand side is from RTT with intensive property $\rho e$, where $e$ is the energy per mass. What types of energy are represented within $e$?

::: {.callout-note collapse="true" title="Think about the types of energy first, then click here to reveal"}

We need to account for the kinetic energy per mass, $\tfrac{1}{2}|\mathbf{u}|^2$, the potential energy per mass $gz$, and the internal energy per mass, $c_v T$ (where $c_v$ is the specific heat at constant volume and $T$ is the temperature). That is

$$
e= \tfrac{1}{2}|\mathbf{u}|^2 + gz + c_v T.
$$
:::

What types of **heat** transfer can occur in $\dot{Q}$? You'll learn this in MCEN 3022: Heat Transfer, but the three modes of heat transfer are

- Conduction: heat passes through solid objects
- Convection: a fluid passing over an object will add/remove heat from the object, e.g. blowing on a hot meatball to cool it down.
- Radiation: light (including infrared, visible, ultraviolet, and beyond) carries energy.
- ex: electrical resistance, flame, "red-hot"

What types of **work** can occur in $\dot{W}$?

- viscous work, boundary work (change in volume), turbine (shaft), pump, ...

And we need to consider the amount of work it takes to push a fluid parcel into a control volume. This is called **flow work**, and it is indeed a work, but we will end up grouping it with the energy term in our integral equation because it is always present in flowing systems.

## Flow work

It takes energy to push fluid into a control volume.

**Dimensionally?** "push" $\rightarrow$ pressure, needs a rate... $U$ or $Q$?

$$
\underset{\color{red}{\frac{F\cdot L}{T}}}{\dot{W}} = \underset{\color{red}{\frac{F}{L^2}\cdot\frac{L^3}{T}}}{P\cdot Q} \qquad \checkmark
$$

**Simple example**

How much work is necessary to push the <span style="color:#1f77e0">blue</span> slug into the <span style="color:#e0311f">red</span> CV?

$$
(P\cdot A)\cdot L
$$

... and then we make it continuous (per time)

$$
\rightarrow (P\cdot A)\cdot U = P\cdot Q
$$

So: the flow work will be...

$$
\begin{aligned}
\dot{W}_\text{flow} &= -\int P\, \mathbf{u}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{n}}\, dS_\text{in} - \int P\, \mathbf{u}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{n}}\, dS_\text{out} \\
&= -\int_{CS} P\, \mathbf{u}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{n}}\, dS
\end{aligned}
$$

So, conservation of energy looks like

::: {.callout-important title="Conservation of Energy (Integral Form)"}
$$
\dot{Q} + \dot{W} = \int_{CV} \frac{\partial}{\partial t}(\rho e)\, dV + \int_{CS} \rho\left(e + \frac{P}{\rho}\right)(\mathbf{u}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{n}})\, dS
$$

for

$$
e = \tfrac{1}{2}|\mathbf{u}|^2 + gz + c_v T
$$
:::

**Assumption:** $z$, $P$, $\rho$, & $T$ are uniform across the inlet face and outlet face. (And will do a trick with $|\mathbf{u}|^2$ as well.)

Let's also assume steady flow.

$$
\begin{aligned}
\dot{Q} + \dot{W} &= \cancelto{0}{\int_{CV} \frac{\partial}{\partial t}(\rho e)\, dV} + \int_{CS} \rho\left(\tfrac{1}{2}|\mathbf{u}|^2 + gz + c_v T + \frac{P}{\rho}\right)(\mathbf{u}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{n}})\, dS \\
&= \left(gz + c_v T + \frac{P}{\rho}\right)_\text{in} \int \rho\, \mathbf{u}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{n}}\, dS_\text{in} + \int \tfrac{1}{2}\rho|\mathbf{u}|^2\, \mathbf{u}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{n}}\, dS_\text{in} \\
&\quad + (\text{same for "out"}) \\
&= -\dot{m}\left(gz + c_v T + \frac{P}{\rho}\right)_\text{in} + \rho\, \underbrace{\int \tfrac{1}{2}|\mathbf{u}|^2\, \mathbf{u}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{n}}\, dS_\text{in}}_{\color{red}{\downarrow}} \\
&\quad + (\text{same for "out"})
\end{aligned}
$$

Typically, we will see one of these three flows:

1) Uniform flow, $\mathbf{u} = U_0\,\hat{\mathbf{z}}$
2) Parabolic flow, $\mathbf{u} = U_\text{max}\left(1 - \left(\frac{r}{R}\right)^2\right)\hat{\mathbf{z}}$
3) Turbulent flow, $\mathbf{u} \approx U_0\,\hat{\mathbf{z}}$ (statistically)

$\longrightarrow$ Catalogue the values of the integration and characterize the flows w/ "the kinetic energy coefficient"

$$
\alpha \equiv \frac{\int \tfrac{1}{2}\rho|\mathbf{u}|^2\, \mathbf{u}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{n}}\, dS}{\tfrac{1}{2}\dot{m}\,\underset{\color{red}{\uparrow \text{ avg speed}}}{\bar{U}^2}}
$$

<span style="color:#e0311f">(example below, but...)</span>

| $\alpha$ | |
|:-:|:--|
| $1$ | for uniform flows |
| $2$ | for parabolic flows |
| $\approx 1$ | for turbulent flows (0.95?) |

For pipe-like flows, the conservation of energy becomes:

::: {.callout-important title="Conservation of Energy (Pipe-Like Flows)"}
$$
\begin{aligned}
\dot{Q} + \dot{W} = \dot{m}\Bigg[&\left(\tfrac{1}{2}\alpha\, U_\text{avg}^2 + gz + c_v T + \frac{P}{\rho}\right)_\text{out} \\
-&\left(\tfrac{1}{2}\alpha\, U_\text{avg}^2 + gz + c_v T + \frac{P}{\rho}\right)_\text{in}\Bigg]
\end{aligned}
$$
:::

## For the curious

Parabolic flow $\longrightarrow$ $u(r) = U_\text{max}\left(1 - \left(\frac{r}{R}\right)^2\right)$

::: {.column-margin}
<span style="color:#e0311f">We will see how this ($U_\text{max}$) depends on applied pressure.</span>
:::

$$
\bar{U} = \frac{\displaystyle\int_0^{2\pi}\!\!\int_0^R U_\text{max}\left(1 - \left(\frac{r}{R}\right)^2\right) r\, dr\, d\theta}{\pi R^2} = \frac{U_\text{max}\cdot\frac{\pi}{2}R^2}{\pi R^2}
$$

$$
\therefore\quad \text{Avg speed} = \bar{U} = U_\text{max}/2
$$

$$
\begin{aligned}
\alpha \equiv \frac{\int \tfrac{1}{2}\rho|\mathbf{u}|^2\, \mathbf{u}\cdot\hat{\mathbf{n}}\, dS}{\tfrac{1}{2}\dot{m}\,\bar{U}^2}
&= \frac{\tfrac{1}{2}\rho \displaystyle\int_0^{2\pi}\!\!\int_0^R \left[U_\text{max}\left(1 - \left(\frac{r}{R}\right)^2\right)\right]^3 r\, dr\, d\theta}{\tfrac{1}{2}\left(\rho\cdot\pi R^2\cdot\bar{U}\right)\bar{U}^2} \\
&= \frac{\cancel{\tfrac{1}{2}}\cancel{\rho}\,(2\cancel{\pi})\, U_\text{max}^3\, \frac{\cancel{R^2}}{8}}{\cancel{\tfrac{1}{2}}\cancel{\rho}\,\cancel{\pi}\cancel{R^2}\,\bar{U}^3} \\
&= \frac{2\,(2\bar{U})^3}{8\,\bar{U}^3} = 2
\end{aligned}
$$

$$
\therefore\quad \alpha = 2 \text{ for parabolic flow}
$$
